absent: There is no Latin American participatory-research lineage at all - no Freire, Fals Borda or Santos - so 'partnership' arrives with no ecology-of-knowledges or PAR grounding, and the decolonial reading runs almost entirely through anglophone UK sources with Mignolo (2018) as the lone exception.
forYou: The move here - taking a partnership technology built for engagement and asking it to carry an epistemic argument - is the same structural bet you are making when you locate professional criticality in an ecosystem rather than in an individual, and it is worth holding up at CARN 2026 when 'Substrate Matters' asks what a partnership is actually growing in.
method: References from Crossref; strands and narrative by Claude, grounded only in the reference list and title. 22 of the 61 references carry a DOI and nothing else in Crossref, and the batch DOI lookup returned unrelated records this run, so those 22 are omitted rather than guessed.
narrative:
The oldest layer in this reference list is not education at all. Miller (1961) on dividend policy and Hull (2009) on derivatives sit there as the canon the paper reads against - the finance and business teaching, extended by Heath (2018) and Crane (2019), that the authors treat as colonial by default rather than by intent. Against that sits a decolonial tradition entering UK higher education through Tuck (2012), Ahmed (2012) and Dei (2017), consolidating around Bhambra (2018), Andrews (2018) and Mignolo (2018), and reaching the disciplines with Moncrieffe (2020), Adebisi (2024) and Gilani (2024).

A second strand is empirical and institutional. Bhopal (2018), Arday (2018), Sian (2019), Andrews (2021) and Joseph-Salisbury (2021) document racism inside British universities, with Universities UK (2020) and the Office for Students (2022) supplying the official record. From 2024 this turns into case work - Davis (2024) in Welsh initial teacher education, Tamimi (2024) at a UK university, Memon (2025) at Cardiff - which is the genre this paper joins.

The third strand is older and was developed separately: students as partners, via Thomas (2012), Cook-Sather (2014) and Healey (2014). The paper's actual move is to graft that machinery onto the decolonial argument, a join already being attempted by Araneta (2022, 2025). Race (2022) and Pillay (2022) mark the live disagreement it enters - whether decolonising means changing what is on the reading list or what counts as knowledge - with Banks (2019) as the multicultural-education precursor the decolonial writers define themselves against.
